title: Hymns of the Companions to Sri Gaura
html:
Stotras of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and Rupa Gosvami, the Shikshashtaka and other verses of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

Translated from the Sanskrit

✦

Translator's Preface

This small volume gathers the Sanskrit hymns (stotras) composed about Sri Chaitanya by two of His closest disciples — Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami — together with the eight verses He composed Himself. They are among the earliest and most reliable testimonies to Mahaprabhu: Rupa saw Him at Prayaga, in Vrindavana and in Puri; Raghunatha lived with Him in Puri for some sixteen years under the care of Svarupa Damodara and witnessed His last years — those pastimes of divine madness in separation from Krishna which Krishnadasa Kaviraja later described, from the accounts of Raghunatha and Svarupa, in the Antya-lila of the Chaitanya-charitamrita. Kaviraja Gosvami repeatedly quotes these stotras and builds his narrative on them.

Contents of the volume.
1. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, from the collection Stava-vali ("Garland of Hymns"): the Shachisunv-ashtaka (in
Puridasa's edition, "Sri Chaitanyashtaka"), the Sri Gauranga-stava-kalpataru, and six separate verses on Gaura
from other stotras — the Manah-shiksha, the Vilapa-kusumanjali and others.
2. Rupa Gosvami, from the collection Stava-mala ("Wreath of Hymns", compiled by Jiva Gosvami): the three
Chaitanyashtakas with which the collection opens.
3. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the Shikshashtaka ("Eight Verses of Instruction"), preserved by Rupa in his anthology
Padyavali, and two further verses signed there with His name.

Sixty-four verses in all. A detailed catalogue is in `CATALOG.md`.

Sources. The Stava-mala — the Kāvyamālā edition, no. 84 (Bombay, Nirnaya Sagar, 1903); the Padyavali — the edition of Ramanarayana Vidyaratna (Berhampore, 1911); the Stava-vali — the Sanskrit text of Puridasa's critical edition (Dacca, 1947), checked against the Gaudiya Grantha Mandira e-text (no early edition of the Stava-vali was found in the public domain). Only the sixteenth-century Sanskrit text is translated; the commentaries of these editions (on the Stava-mala, ascribed in the edition to Jiva Gosvami; on the Padyavali, by Virachandra Gosvami) were used only to understand difficult passages, and where an interpretation rests on them this is stated in the notes. Variant readings are recorded in the notes.

Principles of translation. Only the text is translated, without the original or a word-for-word gloss; one verse is one paragraph under its number, as in the original (the phala-shruti is the last verse of a stotra). The stotras are written in strict classical metres (shikharini, prithvi); the translation is in prose, without rhyme or metre, but the refrains repeated in each verse are kept. Double meanings (shlesha), realia and parallels with the Chaitanya-charitamrita (CC) are explained in the notes. Theological explanations follow the tradition of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati: Sri Gaura is Krishna Himself, who took the bhava and lustre of Radha in order to taste the sweetness of Her love; His "madness" in separation is the highest manifestation of mahabhava, not a worldly disorder; the love of the gopis of which these hymns speak has nothing in common with worldly passion. Names and terms follow `GLOSSARY.md`.

✦
